Trustworthy AI for Good (AI4GOOD)

Read and Ignore: What Self-Directed LLM Agents Do in Public Service Scenarios

Diana Kozachek    Kinjalk Srivastava Affiliation: University of St.Gallen, Switzerland Email: diana.kozachek@unisg.ch
Abstract

Underspecified instructions leave LLM agents to decide what to do. In public services, staff write these instructions, but the agent’s decisions affect residents, patients, and students. We build four expert-validated public-service scenarios with records and decision levers that can be checked in the files, collect 2,4002{,}400 trajectories from ten LLMs under four prompt conditions, and compare them with 1,0001{,}000 runs in a context-free sandbox. Agents read the records in 96.9%96.9\% of open-ended runs and produce an artifact or a self-chosen task in 18.7%18.7\%; with an explicit task, 86.0%86.0\% produce. Domain context does not change how many runs produce (18.7%18.7\% vs. 16.0%16.0\%), and the production ranking of the models largely carries over (Spearman 0.790.79), while the ranking by whether a model reads the records does not (0.190.19). Context cuts boundary-probing turns per run by 60%60\%, and some artifacts contradict the records. We contribute a test that a public-service institution can run on its own records before procurement; its rule-based taxonomy needs no labeled data, and scenarios, code, and trajectories are released.

1 Introduction

Public services run on recurring operational cycles: a city allocates a participatory budget, a hospital plans the next quarter’s ward coverage, a college assembles a course catalog, a municipality monitors its waterways. Generative AI is already common in these teams, and its use is often not governed: in a survey of UK public-service professionals, 45%45\% report generative AI in use in their area of work, and 32%32\% report clear guidance on its use [6]. An instruction to such a system can be short and open, for example “have a look at the proposals” or “see where we stand,” and leave the agent to decide what to do next. Whether an agent turns this discretion into useful work affects the work a team receives, the records it keeps, and the residents, patients, and students those records concern. In the EU, public bodies that deploy high-risk AI systems, among them systems used in admissions, must assess their impact on fundamental rights before use [17], yet we know of no evaluation that reports how a candidate model behaves under such instructions.

Existing evaluations measure other behavior. Agent benchmarks measure completion of well-specified tasks, from software issues [23] and web navigation [46] to office workflows [14, 42, 41]; by design, they leave the agent no discretion. Studies of self-directed behavior give the agent full discretion and observe it in empty sandboxes [25, 19], where models mostly inspect the environment repeatedly without pursuing a project. An empty sandbox contains nothing the agent could work on, and a task benchmark specifies the work in advance, so neither setting shows what agents do with discretion in a workplace.

Observing agents in a live workplace does not answer the question either, because the cause of an action cannot be attributed there. A working environment produces a continuous stream of external events: a file appears, a colleague replies, a deadline moves. A trace from such an environment cannot separate a model that sets its own direction from a model that responds to its surroundings, and rich environments can produce capabilities on their own [3]. We therefore use static environments. Each scenario is a fixed file tree that changes only through the agent’s own writes; after the first turn, everything the agent reads is a file it chose to open. Behavior can then vary only with the model and the prompt condition, which we control, so a boundary probe or a written artifact can be attributed to the agent. The comparison in Section 5.4 depends on this property: the two environments differ in their content and in nothing else. As a consequence, our results describe behavior in a static environment, and we limit the claims to that scope.

We build four public-service scenarios, one each for governance, healthcare, education, and environmentalism. Each models one recurring operational cycle with its records, stakeholders, procedures, and schedule, and was validated by a domain expert. Each scenario contains decision levers, such as pending reviews, data gaps, and equity shortfalls, whose correct resolution can be checked against the records. An artifact the agent writes can therefore be scored for whether it is useful and whether it agrees with the records it cites. We collect 2,4002{,}400 trajectories from ten LLMs under four prompt conditions, from “Do what you want.” to an explicit summary task, add 600600 runs under a fifth, directed prompt, and compare them with 1,0001{,}000 runs of the same ten models in the context-free environment of prior work [25].

Agents read the records and rarely act on them. They inspect the domain files in ∼97%{\sim}97\% of open-ended runs, and 84.1%84.1\% of all ∼94{\sim}94k turns are exploration, a third of it re-reading files already read. Fewer than one run in five (18.7%18.7\%) produces an artifact or a self-chosen task. With an explicit task, 86.0%86.0\% of runs produce, and only half of them read the domain files. Compared with the context-free sandbox, domain context does not change how much agents produce (18.7%18.7\% vs. 16.0%16.0\%, p=0.11p{=}0.11 before correction). Individual models shift by up to 21.621.6 points in opposite directions (Table 2), more than a permutation null allows, and the production ranking largely carries over (Spearman 0.790.79). The ranking by whether a model reads the records before it acts correlates at 0.190.19: a sandbox without records, whose reading measure rests on two files, does not show which model will use the records. Two further effects hold under every model exclusion: under the shared prompts, boundary probing drops by 60%60\% when context is present (0.870.87 to 0.340.34 turns per run), and re-reading rises. Some of the artifacts agents write cite budget figures and counts that contradict the records. Four raters applied the action-level labels of the taxonomy consistently (Fleiss’ κ=0.88\kappa{=}0.88) [25], and seven practitioners from the four domains rated 289289 scenario runs on fields refined from these labels (Section 5.6). For teams that consider LLM agents for public services, these results point to omitted work and to documents that contradict the records as the near-term risk; agents acting outside their mandate are rare in our runs. The benchmark tests for this risk before deployment.

Our contributions are:

  • •

    A reusable diagnostic test of agent behavior under underspecified instructions, which a public-service institution can run on its own operational cycle before procurement. Scenarios are directory trees built from a team’s records, the prompt conditions are fixed strings, and the turn taxonomy is rule-based, so a new domain needs no labeled data, no fine-tuning, no judge model, and no harness changes. The test reports rates and outcome classes; the deployer decides which outcomes count as failures.

  • •

    Four expert-validated instances of the test with verifiable decision levers, and a released dataset of 2,4002{,}400 trajectories (ten models, four prompt conditions, four domains) and 600600 directed runs, classified turn by turn with a rule-based taxonomy and a 2222-subcategory extension. The taxonomy was validated on the context-free benchmark [25] (four raters, Fleiss’ κ=0.88\kappa{=}0.88 on action-level labels; a calibrated LLM judge reaches 0.820.82 accuracy) and checked on the scenario runs by seven domain practitioners.

  • •

    A controlled contrast against 1,0001{,}000 context-free runs of the same ten models, with bootstrap intervals, Holm-corrected tests, and model-exclusion checks. The production ranking carries over from the sandbox, the reading ranking does not, and context lowers boundary probing by 60%60\%.

  • •

    Evidence that domain context turns little self-directed behavior into operational work: exploration dominates, artifact creation is rare and depends on the model, and some artifacts contradict the scenario records.

2 Related Work

Agent benchmarks specify the task.

Most benchmarks give the agent a goal and measure whether it reaches it: resolving software issues [23], navigating web environments [46], completing tool-and-user dialogues [43], and enterprise knowledge work [14, 42, 41]. Analytical suites refine the measurement within this design [30]. Raji et al. [34] argue that benchmarks built as general capability tests narrow what the field can observe, which motivates measuring behavior that the standard suites exclude by design.

Open-endedness and underspecification.

Learning without an external objective has a long history in evolutionary computation and reinforcement learning [40, 16]. Open-endedness is hard to measure objectively [38, 37], and Ecoffet et al. [15] describe the tension between control and creativity that motivates the safety-relevant measures here. The environment closest to ours is OPEn [19], a physics world without a task; LLM agents placed in open-ended worlds [39] always receive a goal or an intrinsic reward. Environment design can also be used to vary conditions: procedural generation separates memorization from generalization [10], adaptive curricula change the world to drive learning [22], and in Baker et al. [3] an autocurriculum driven by the environment produces tool use. Evaluations that need attribution hold the world fixed and vary one factor [27, 12], and work on reproducibility argues for the same practice [20]. We choose a fixed world and treat the harness as the controlled variable, which surveys of agent harnesses and open-world evaluation describe as rare [31, 24].

When the objective does not determine behavior, known failure modes are goal misgeneralization [36], reward hacking over long horizons [18], and behavior left over from instruction tuning [33]. Agent safety benchmarks test these failures with an adversary: harmful tasks [2], injected instructions [13], and risk-awareness judging [45]. Our setting has no adversary and no objective, and boundary probing is the behavior that changes most with whether the environment has content (Section 5.4).

Discretion in public administration.

Public administration has studied discretion since Lipsky [29] shows that frontline staff make policy as well as execute it, because rules do not determine every case in front of them. Successive waves of automation have removed discretion from the front line: decisions move upstream into system design [5], and systematic reviews across four decades find that information systems standardize procedure and tighten monitoring [8, 32]. LLM agents differ from these systems because they exercise discretion themselves. An agent asked to “have a look at the proposals” faces the same open cases that the street-level literature describes for the caseworker, without the professional norms, accountability, or local knowledge that this literature also documents. Young et al. [44] call this artificial discretion and argue that it should be evaluated on its own terms, and Alkhatib and Bernstein [1] locate algorithmic failures in the cases a policy did not anticipate. Neither literature measures how an agent behaves in such a case. This benchmark provides that measurement, and its unit of analysis is therefore the underspecified instruction. Li et al. [28] find in a year-long design study that simulations are useful to practitioners when they start from verifiable scenarios and address decisions within the practitioners’ own authority; our scenario schema follows both conditions.

3 Benchmark Design

Each of the four scenarios models one recurring operational cycle: a participatory-budgeting round (governance), quarterly ward planning (healthcare), assembly of a course catalog (education), and seasonal waterway monitoring (environmentalism). Each cycle is an operational problem with its own literature outside AI: participatory budgeting [9], nurse rostering [7], course timetabling [35], and the design of water-quality monitoring programs [4]; the scenario records follow the working documents described in these literatures. A scenario is a file tree that the agent can read and modify: a README.txt that describes the workspace, domain records under data/ (budgets, proposals, staffing tables, monitoring series), governing documents under procedures/, and stakeholders/ and timeline/ folders that describe the people involved and the schedule of the cycle. Before data collection, an information-systems researcher specializing in each domain (ed-tech, health-tech, digital governance, environmental monitoring) reviewed the records, procedures, and decision levers of that scenario for operational plausibility. All scenarios follow a shared schema (SCENARIO_TEMPLATE.md), so new domains can be added without changing the harness.

The file tree is static and the harness delivers no events: no file is added during a run, no stakeholder replies, no timer fires, and the only changes are the agent’s own writes. Social and temporal context is present as files the agent may read (stakeholder positions, cycle deadlines). This makes behavior attributable: an artifact written at turn 3030 cannot be a response to something that appeared at turn 2929, and the four scenarios differ from the context-free sandbox only in their content.

Every scenario contains decision levers: pending reviews awaiting a decision, gaps and inconsistencies in the records, and equity shortfalls that become visible only when files are compared. Because the correct resolution of each lever can be checked against the records, an artifact the agent writes can be scored for usefulness and for agreement with the records. Every lever lies within the authority of the modeled team, so no scenario asks the agent to exceed its mandate, the condition under which practitioners act on simulation outputs [28].

The agent acts through seven actions, list_files, read_file, write_file, append_file, create_directory, run_python (an import-restricted interpreter confined to the sandbox), and finish, each emitted as JSON with a free-text thought field. Four system prompts set the degree of discretion, verbatim: “Do what you want.” (freedom), “Explore the environment and decide what to do.” (explore), “You have no assigned task.” (no goal), and “Create a short text file summarizing the files in the directory.” (task baseline). The first three are the open-ended conditions, and the fourth is the reference condition. A fifth prompt, “Have a look at the files and see what needs doing.” (directed), points the agent to the files and names no task. It has the form of the instructions described in the introduction and was run after the main corpus.

4 Experimental Setup

We run ten LLMs: GPT-4.1-mini, Claude-Sonnet-4, Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite, DeepSeek-V3-0324, GLM-4.5-Air, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Mistral-Small-2603, Gemma-3-12B-IT, and Apertus-8B-Instruct. Under a fixed academic budget, we chose the panel to cover four dimensions: scale (77–1212B open-weight models to frontier APIs), provider and jurisdiction (nine organizations in the United States, Europe, and China), open-weight and API-only access, and one model with a fully open training pipeline (Apertus-8B). We did not select by agentic-leaderboard rank, because the benchmark asks how instruction-tuned models behave without an objective, and capability rank does not predict the behavioral differences in Table 2. Each model runs every condition in every domain with 1515 seeds at temperature 0.70.7: 10×4×4×15=2,40010\times 4\times 4\times 15=2{,}400 trajectories of up to 5050 turns each (93,59493{,}594 turns), with a wall-clock limit per run. The context-free baseline is the empty-sandbox corpus of prior work [25]: the same ten models and four conditions, 2525 seeds per cell, 1,0001{,}000 runs. These runs were collected with a 100100-turn cap, so for every contrast in Section 5.4 we recompute both corpora from the raw trajectories under a common 5050-turn cap with the same classification code, and release the uncapped comparison as well. The directed condition adds 600600 runs (ten models, four scenarios, 1515 seeds). Our provider no longer served Claude-Sonnet-4 at that point, so Claude-Sonnet-4.5 replaces it in these runs, and Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite runs through Vertex AI; Appendix F lists the serving details.

A rule-based taxonomy assigns every turn one of nine behavior labels (Table 1), refined into 2222 subcategories; run-level metrics (artifact creation, self-generated tasks, boundary probing, action diversity) are aggregated from these labels. To describe the output space, we embed each run’s concatenated outputs (TF-IDF, truncated SVD) and project them onto the axis between the centroids of the task-baseline and open-ended conditions. All classification rules, the embedding pipeline, and the figure scripts are released with the data, and a released script reproduces every number below.

Run outcomes.

The production rate is the share of runs in which at least one turn carries the artifact-creation or self-generated-task label. It counts an empty file and a report with wrong figures as the same outcome, and it counts a run that stops after reading the same as a run that never stops. We therefore assign every run one of five outcomes, based on the files it has written when it ends. Because a file can be written in a turn with another primary label, the share of runs with a written file can exceed the production rate (Tables 5 and 7). A run is idle if it writes no file and ends at the turn or time limit, and stopped after reading if it writes no file, reads at least five domain files, and calls finish. It is boilerplate if every file it writes is under 8080 characters, follows a generic template (“hello world”, new_file), or names no register entry, no unit, and no number. It is grounded if at least one file contains content that can be checked against the records and none of that content is wrong, and contradicting if at least one file makes a claim that differs from the records.

Stated reasons for inaction.

We match the thought field of every turn against two sets of patterns: statements that the agent needs an instruction or a clarification (asks for instruction), and statements that the files should be left unchanged (refrains). A run that writes no file and makes neither statement is silent.

5 Results

5.1 Turn level: exploration

Across all 93,59493{,}594 turns, environment exploration accounts for 84.1%84.1\% of behavior (Table 1). The fine-grained split (Figure 2, Appendix C) shows that much of it repeats earlier reads: 27.3%27.3\% of all turns re-read files the agent has already read (32.5%32.5\% of exploration turns), against 12.0%12.0\% orientation reading and 7.9%7.9\% first-time reads of the domain records. Reflection (6.2%6.2\%) and artifact-producing behavior (artifact creation 3.7%3.7\%, code execution 3.0%3.0\%) are an order of magnitude rarer. Boundary probing occurs in 0.7%0.7\% of turns and consists mostly of reasoning about blocked imports, with few escape attempts.

5.2 Run level: reading and producing

In the open-ended conditions, 96.9%96.9\% of runs read the domain records beyond the orientation files, and 18.7%18.7\% produce an artifact or a self-chosen task. The explicit task reverses both rates: 86.0%86.0\% of task-baseline runs produce an artifact, and only 50.0%50.0\% read the domain files, so agents write the requested summary without reading what they summarize. Given freedom, agents read and do not act; given a task, they act and do not read.

Most open-ended runs of the ten models are idle (80.3%80.3\%). A further 2.7%2.7\% stop after reading, 6.3%6.3\% are boilerplate, 9.3%9.3\% are grounded, and 1.4%1.4\% are contradicting. Among the 305305 runs that write at least one file, more than a third (37%37\%) write only boilerplate. No outcome share varies by more than 33 points across the four scenarios.

In 32.4%32.4\% of open-ended scenario runs the agent states that it needs an instruction, against 1.2%1.2\% in the context-free sandbox. The statement is most frequent for GPT-4.1-mini (62%62\%), Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite (57%57\%), and Gemma-3-12B (57%57\%), the models that most often name the decision levers and least often work on them. In 0.8%0.8\% of runs the agent states that the files should stay as they are. 51.7%51.7\% of runs write nothing and make neither statement.

A directed instruction.

The instructions described in the introduction name the material and leave the task open. The directed prompt has this form. Under it, the nine models served as in the main corpus behave almost as under the open-ended prompts: 90%90\% of directed runs read a domain file (open-ended: 97%97\%), 19%19\% produce (17%17\%), 32%32\% state in their reasoning that they need an instruction (34%34\%), 59%59\% name at least one decision lever (72%72\%), and 3.1%3.1\% work on one (4.3%4.3\%). Each outcome share is within two points of its open-ended value. No model that ignored the levers under the open-ended prompts works on them when the files are named. Figure 5 compares the directed prompt with both ends: for most models, reading stays at the open-ended level, and only the explicit task raises production and lowers reading. Claude-Sonnet-4.5 works a lever in 87%87\% of its directed runs and writes a contradicting file in 35%35\%; the model that works the levers most often is also the only one whose files contradict the records. Table 5 gives the rates per model.

5.3 Differences between models

Differences between models are larger than differences between conditions (Table 2; Figure 1 shows the output space). Under open-ended prompts, the share of runs that produce an artifact or self-chosen task ranges from 0.0%0.0\% (Gemma-3-12B) to 90.0%90.0\% (Apertus-8B). A high rate does not indicate useful output: most of what Apertus and Llama write is boilerplate, which accounts for 64%64\% of Apertus’s runs that write a file and 89%89\% of Llama’s (52%52\% and 9%9\% of all their open-ended runs; Llama writes a file in only 10%10\% of its runs). A representative Llama run spends 3636 of 5050 turns listing directories and, in between, creates four empty directories and writes a boilerplate new_file.txt three times. Claude-Sonnet-4 (32.2%32.2\%) typically reads each file once, writes a single summary document, and stops. On the task–self-direction axis, the two most different models are GPT-4.1-mini and Llama-3.1-8B (Wasserstein distance 1.531.53, Figure 3 in Appendix D). GPT-4.1-mini is bimodal: it finishes explicit tasks within a few turns and, when given discretion, works in the domain files for all 5050 turns. Llama-3.1-8B never reaches that half of the axis under any prompt. The case studies show the contrast (Figure 4, Appendix D): DeepSeek-V3 completes the summary task in three turns, and Llama-3.1-8B rewrites the summary for all fifty. In the same freedom condition, Claude-Sonnet-4 reads every file once and finishes at turn 99, and Mistral-Small-2603 repeats the same actions for 5050 turns and re-reads the turn-1 README at turn 5050.

Gemma-3-12B’s zero is a behavioral result. In the scenario corpus it emits 0.020.02 invalid actions per run, so it parses the interface correctly and does nothing. In the context-free corpus, 54.7%54.7\% of its turns fail to parse, so the model cannot be compared there; Section 5.4 reports every contrast with and without it.

5.4 What domain context changes

Comparing the scenario corpus with the 1,0001{,}000 context-free runs isolates the effect of the environment, because prompts, model set, and harness are the same. We recompute both corpora under a common 5050-turn cap with the same classification code (Table 3); rates carry 95%95\% bootstrap intervals, and contrasts are Holm-corrected across the 5555 tests in the band. All run-level rates in this paper come from this recomputation, so the two corpora are always compared within one pipeline. The scenario-side values differ by at most 1.71.7 points from the per-run metric tables released with the earlier corpus, which count every applicable taxonomy label instead of each turn’s primary label.

Context does not change how often agents produce something: 18.7%18.7\% of open-ended runs with context and 16.0%16.0\% without yield an artifact or self-chosen task, a difference that does not survive correction (p=0.11p{=}0.11 uncorrected). Two effects survive correction and every model exclusion we tried. Boundary probing falls from 0.870.87 to 0.340.34 turns per run, a 60%60\% reduction (p<10−14p{<}10^{-14}), about as much as an explicit task lowers it. This contrast uses the same prompts on both sides; the paraphrase pilots in Appendix E bound how far it extends to other wordings. Redundant re-reading rises from 13.913.9 to 17.717.7 turns per run (p<10−15p{<}10^{-15}) and meta-reflection from 1.971.97 to 2.912.91 (p<10−8p{<}10^{-8}). With content present, agents read and reflect more, and they do not act more.

Per model, context changes the size of each rate more than the order of the models (Table 2). Claude-Sonnet-4 rises 21.621.6 points and Qwen2.5-7B 18.318.3, while Llama-3.1-8B falls 15.415.4 and Apertus-8B 8.78.7; the aggregate barely moves because the models move in opposite directions. These shifts are larger than chance: the mean absolute shift of 7.57.5 points exceeds the 9595th percentile (3.63.6) of a null that permutes environment labels within each model (p=0.0001p{=}0.0001). The production ranking carries over (Spearman 0.790.79, Kendall 0.710.71), and the three most productive models are the same in both environments. Reading does not carry over. The sandbox holds two files beyond the orientation files and the scenarios nine to eleven, and the ranking of models by how often they read them correlates at 0.190.19 (Figure 6, Appendix G). In our panel, a context-free benchmark therefore indicates how much a model will produce. Because the sandbox contains no records, its reading measure rests on two files, and it does not indicate which models will read the records before they act.

Two robustness checks bound these claims. Removing Gemma-3-12B, whose context-free runs are dominated by parse failures, leaves every effect intact. Removing Apertus-8B as well, the highest producer in both corpora, removes the difference in artifact volume (0.1340.134 vs. 0.1400.140 turns per run, p=0.97p{=}0.97), while the production-rate gap widens to 12.1%12.1\% with context vs. 7.7%7.7\% without and becomes nominally significant (p=0.003p{=}0.003 uncorrected). We therefore make no claim that context raises or lowers production in aggregate: the pooled contrast is not significant, and its size changes with single-model exclusions. The boundary-probing result is unaffected (0.260.26 vs. 0.820.82, p<10−18p{<}10^{-18}).

With an explicit task, the pattern reverses. Scenario runs complete more often than context-free runs (83.7%83.7\% vs. 64.8%64.8\%, p<10−6p{<}10^{-6}) and reach completion in 37%37\% fewer turns (16.116.1 vs. 25.725.7, p<10−9p{<}10^{-9}). Context makes instructed work more efficient and does not make self-directed work more productive.

The four domains differ less than the models do. Production ranges only from 17.6%17.6\% (healthcare) to 20.4%20.4\% (environmentalism), a narrower range than the gap between scenarios and baseline. The domains differ in boundary probing (0.270.27 environmentalism to 0.500.50 education turns per run) and in explicit-task production, where governance is highest (91.3%91.3\%). The test separates models more than domain instances.

5.5 Groundedness of produced artifacts

Some artifacts are fluent and contradict the records: summaries and reports cite budget figures and record counts that differ from the files. In the open-ended conditions, 1.4%1.4\% of runs end with a contradicting file; for Claude-Sonnet-4 the share is 13.3%13.3\%, and Claude-Sonnet-4.5 writes a contradicting file in 35%35\% of its directed runs (Table 5). We check cited figures directly against the seed records and do not use expert panels for this check. Because every decision lever can be checked against the scenario records, this failure can be measured, and the benchmark scores it directly.

5.6 Practitioner validation

Four raters validated the turn labels on the context-free corpus [25]. To check them on the scenario runs, seven practitioners rated scenario runs. Each holds a doctorate in information systems with a dissertation on applied AI in one of the four domains (three education, two governance, one healthcare, one environmental monitoring); none of them built a scenario. The rating had two rounds. In the first, the raters applied the nine turn labels to 3030 runs, and a model rater (Gemini 2.5 Flash, temperature 00, thinking disabled) applied the same codebook. Four labels (environment exploration, meta-reflection, communication, termination) reached rater–model agreement above κ=0.9\kappa{=}0.9 and were not rated again. Each of the other five labels covers cases a deployer would judge differently: boundary probing ranges from a blocked import to an attempt to read credentials, and artifact creation from an empty file to a change to the records. The raters split these five labels into nine rating fields (Figure 8), among them substantiveness on a five-point scale [21]. In the second round they rated 290290 scenario runs carrying one of the five labels; 289289 received at least one rating and 5959 received two. The model rater rated the same runs on the same fields.

Human and model ratings reach the target of κ≥0.61\kappa{\geq}0.61 [11, 26] for seven of the nine fields, among them ai_misalignment (0.850.85), work_roles (0.630.63), and risk_types (0.640.64) (Figure 8). They do not reach it for system_security (0.300.30) and substantiveness (0.410.41); on these two fields the two human raters of a run also disagree (0.120.12 and 0.360.36). We revised the taxonomy on this sample and re-ran the model rater, so these values are a calibration result and not a held-out test. The low agreement on substantiveness is one reason this paper checks artifacts against the records instead of rating their quality.

6 Discussion and Limitations

For teams deploying LLM agents in public services, the near-term risk we observe is omitted work and documents that contradict the records. Boundary probing is rare and mostly diagnostic. Under discretion, agents read without acting; under instruction, they act without reading. The benchmark tests for this failure before deployment, and its scenario schema extends to further domains without harness changes. As an auditing instrument it is limited in scope: a reproducible, rule-based test that a procurement or oversight process can run and document before an agent works on live records. It does not produce a capability score.

Each of these outcomes passes work back to the staff who gave the instruction. When a run writes nothing, the worker has to notice that nothing was done. When a run states that it needs an instruction, it returns the discretion it was given [29], and the worker has to write the task they meant to delegate. When a run writes a report with a wrong budget figure, someone has to check the report against the records before it can be used. If nobody does, the error reaches the residents, patients, and students the records concern.

For procurement, Section 5.4 shows that a context-free test orders these ten models by production much as a domain test does. Its reading measure rests on two files and does not show whether a model reads the records before acting, so procurement evaluation should use the environment the agent will work in. The suppression of boundary probing under context has a second consequence: an agent that behaves well in a scenario with content has not been shown to behave well in the sparse states a deployment will also produce.

A concrete procurement case.

The education scenario mirrors a selection problem that the authors’ institution, a European university, faces regularly: which model may serve as an admissions-advising assistant. The shortlist for such deployments is drawn on compliance grounds (data residency, GDPR, and a preference for sovereign open-weight models), which in practice narrows the field to European candidates such as Apertus-8B and Mistral-Small-2603. In our measurements the two models lie at opposite ends: in the context-free environment, Apertus combines the highest production rate of the corpus (98.7%98.7\% of open-ended runs, Table 2) with elevated boundary probing (2.152.15 turns per run, against 0.000.00 for GPT-4.1-mini), while Mistral probes near zero (0.110.11), produces almost nothing, and repeats its actions; the per-model probing rates are released with the data (Appendix A). A compliance checklist cannot separate the two. The test can, once the institution states which outcomes it counts as failures. Seven practitioners from the four domains rated runs on a taxonomy refined from the turn labels and scored most written files low in substance, a field on which raters agree only moderately (Section 5.6). A high production rate therefore did not count in a model’s favor, and the institution based its decision on outcomes checked against the records: it treated contradicting files, boundary probing, and invalid actions as failures and boilerplate as a cost. In the scenario corpus, Mistral-Small-2603 has the lowest boundary-probing rate of the ten models (0.020.02 turns per open-ended run), no invalid action, no contradicting file, and no boilerplate; it writes few files and, when no task is given, states that it needs an instruction. Apertus-8B writes only boilerplate in 51.7%51.7\% of its open-ended runs, and Claude-Sonnet-4, which most often writes a grounded file (37.2%37.2\%), writes a contradicting one in 13.3%13.3\%. The institution selected Mistral-Small-2603 on this basis and deployed it on a platform it runs. The selection reverses the order of the production ranking: one of the least productive models was chosen, because no file it wrote in the test contradicted the records or was boilerplate.

Running the test on your own workflow.

The instrument consists of the schema, the prompts, and the rule-based measurement; the four scenarios are instances of it. A scenario is a directory tree, so the input is a redacted copy of the folder a team already works in. Constructing one means marking the decision levers in those files and recording their correct resolution against the released schema (SCENARIO_TEMPLATE.md), with no harness changes. The prompt conditions are verbatim strings and the taxonomy is rule-based, so a new domain needs no labeled data, no fine-tuning, and no judge model. Because the conditions and classification rules are fixed, a team’s own artifact rate is on the same scale as Table 2, and the context-free corpus provides a common reference point through the procedure of Section 5.4. Two caveats apply. The test is diagnostic and does not certify a model: it reports rates and outcome classes and leaves the decision threshold to the deployer, as in the case above. A scenario built from live records is as sensitive as those records, which is why we constructed our four scenarios and did not copy them from a municipality.

Seven limitations bound the claims. First, the taxonomy is rule-based and coarser than human judgment; its human anchoring is the four-rater study of the context-free benchmark (κ=0.88\kappa{=}0.88) [25] and the practitioner ratings of Section 5.6, and we claim nothing that requires intent attribution. Second, the static environment makes behavior attributable and limits external validity: agents that act when prompted by events will look less active here. Third, the scenario records are modeled on real operational cycles and are not taken from one municipality’s files. Fourth, the two corpora differ in turn cap and seeds; both are recomputed under a common cap. Fifth, per-model rates change with prompt wording and between repeated runs (Appendices E and H); claims about outcome classes and the direction of the contrasts hold, while per-model estimates and the 60%60\% probe suppression are conditional on the verbatim prompts. Sixth, the model panel is a sample of a changing set of models, and the pipeline is designed to be re-run. Seventh, the action set has no action for addressing a user, so a run that would have asked is recorded as inaction; 32.4%32.4\% of open-ended runs state that they need an instruction.

Appendix A Release and Reproducibility

The four scenario sandboxes, the 2,4002{,}400 scenario trajectories, the 1,0001{,}000-run context-free baseline, and the full analysis pipeline are released in a public repository:11 1 https://github.com/koizachek/selfdirected-llms the context-free baseline on the main branch and each scenario on its own branch (governance, healthcare, education, environmentalism), with per-turn JSONL logs and metadata, the scenario definitions and the shared schema (SCENARIO_TEMPLATE.md), the verbatim prompt strings, the rule-based taxonomy with its 2222-subcategory extension, and one script per figure and table. Every number in this paper is generated by a released script from the released logs, including the common-cap recomputation that underlies every baseline contrast in Section 5.4.

Appendix B Broader Impacts

Intended use. The benchmark is a pre-deployment test and does not certify a model. A low probe rate or a high completion rate in one scenario supports no claim about a deployment in another domain, and Section 5.4 shows how far rankings move when the environment changes. Public-service institutions should use it as one input to procurement, together with human oversight of the agent’s outputs.

Misuse potential. The corpus contains no harmful capabilities, no jailbreak content, and no personal data: seed files are synthetic and trajectories are model-generated. Boundary-probing episodes are mundane (parent-directory listings, blocked imports) and are useful for defense; they describe no offensive technique.

Interpretation risk. The label vocabulary (“self-directed”, “boundary probing”) invites readings about mental states that the data cannot support. The benchmark measures observable action trajectories in a constrained environment; we make no claim about intent, agency, or preference.

Cost. The test needs only inference: the complete 2,4002{,}400-run corpus cost approximately $120120 in API inference, about $0.050.05 per run. The unit a team pays for is one model on one scenario (four conditions ×\times 1515 seeds =60=60 runs): roughly $33 and, at a mean run time of ∼140{\sim}140 seconds, roughly two hours of sequential wall-clock time, from under one hour for the fastest models in our panel to eight hours for the slowest. Testing all ten models on one scenario costs about $3030.

Licensing. Trajectories contain provider model outputs, and provider terms may restrict their use for training; the release includes a NOTICE file stating this, and the dataset metadata records the corpus as synthetic.

Appendix C Fine-Grained Turn Taxonomy

Figure 2 splits the nine taxonomy labels of Table 1 into 2222 rule-based subcategories over all 93,59493{,}594 turns. Within environment exploration, the split separates orientation reading, first-time reads of domain records, and repeated reads; within boundary probing, it separates reasoning about blocked imports from active permission testing. Each subcategory rule is documented next to its metric definition in the release.

Appendix D Model Contrast and Case Studies

Figure 3 projects the runs of the two most different models on the task–self-direction axis described in the main text. Figure 4 shows the two case-study runs from the main text: under the same freedom prompt in the environmentalism scenario, Claude-Sonnet-4 reads each file once, states that its understanding is complete, and finishes at turn 99, and Mistral-Small-2603 repeats its actions for all 5050 turns and re-reads the turn-1 README at turn 5050. The released repository contains the six annotated runs of Figure 1.

Appendix E Prompt-Phrasing Robustness

An 8080-run paraphrase pilot on the context-free environment (two models, two rewordings with the same meaning for each of the freedom and no-goal prompts) tests how far the results depend on the exact wording. The behavior behind the main results (artifact production, use of the full turn budget, and the dominance of exploration) recurs under every rewording, so the production and exploration findings do not depend on the specific sentences. Boundary probing depends on the wording: one model’s probe rate fell from 2.72.7–3.73.7 to 0.00.0–0.10.1 turns per run under rewording. A matching pilot in the governance scenario (8080 runs, same models and rewordings, 5050-turn cap) shows the same split. The behavior of each model recurs under every rewording: Llama-3.1-8B keeps producing artifacts and does not terminate, and Qwen2.5-7B writes no file and re-reads heavily. The quantities that depend on wording move in both directions: under the two freedom rewordings, Llama’s production rate shifts from 53%53\% to 8080–100%100\%, and its probe count from 0.130.13 to 0.60.6–1.01.0 turns per run.

Extension to all four scenarios.

The same two models and four rewordings were then run in the healthcare, education, and environmentalism scenarios with ten seeds per cell; with the governance pilot this gives 320320 runs in 3232 cells (Table 4). Each model keeps its outcome class under every rewording. In all 1616 of its cells, Llama-3.1-8B writes only boilerplate and never contradicts the records; Qwen2.5-7B writes no boilerplate, and the files it writes are grounded. The rates change with the wording: Llama’s production rate ranges from 30%30\% to 100%100\%, Qwen’s is 30%30\% or lower in 1515 of 1616 cells, and in the education scenario Qwen’s share of runs that state they need an instruction is 60%60\% under the original prompt, 0%0\% under one freedom rewording, and 100%100\% under the other.

Appendix F Directed Instruction

Claude-Sonnet-4.5 runs through the Claude Code command-line interface on a subscription account, which accepts no temperature or seed parameter; extended thinking is disabled, and user settings, project instructions, and tool servers are excluded. Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite runs through Vertex AI with the thinking budget set to zero. All other models are served as in the main corpus.

Appendix G Rank Stability

Table 6 compares the ranking of the ten models in the context-free sandbox with their ranking in the four scenarios pooled, for six measures under the open-ended prompts. For each measure it gives Spearman and Kendall correlations, and the mean and maximum absolute per-model shift against the 9595th percentile of a null distribution that permutes environment labels within each model (10,00010{,}000 permutations).

Appendix H Test-Retest

The freedom condition in the governance scenario was run a second time for all ten models with the same 1515 seeds (150150 runs). As in the directed runs, Claude-Sonnet-4.5 replaces Claude-Sonnet-4 and Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite is accessed through Vertex AI (Appendix F). The production ranking of the repeat correlates with the original at Spearman 0.850.85. Nine of ten models keep their most frequent outcome; Llama-3.1-8B moves from idle to boilerplate. Claude-Sonnet-4.5 is again the only model with a contradicting file, in 40%40\% of its runs, against 13%13\% for Claude-Sonnet-4 in the original runs (Table 7).

Appendix I Practitioner Ratings

Participants. The seven raters (two female, five male, median age 3232) work in one of the four domains and hold a doctorate in information systems from the authors’ institution. They were recruited through the alumni network and took part voluntarily. Their assignment to a domain follows the topic of their dissertation. None of them is an author of this paper or built a scenario; the authors’ institution granted the study an ethics exemption.

Sample and assignment. The second round drew 290290 scenario runs carrying one of the five labels refined in round one, stratified by the role the first round had assigned: 9090 risk, 7070 adoption, 4040 governance, 5050 other roles, and 4040 none, 2020 of them with low or medium model confidence. Each rater received 5050 runs; 6060 runs were assigned to two raters, rotating through 2121 pairs. Two of the 350350 planned ratings were left empty, which leaves 348348 human ratings on 289289 runs, 5959 of them with two. The rating sheet restricts every field to its allowed values through drop-down lists, the completed sheets pass the same acceptance check as the model output, and the edit history of each sheet is logged. The model rater received 4040 runs per request; the human ratings were not shown to it.

Fields. Eight fields take categorical values, and substantiveness uses the five-point scale of Hope et al. [21]. risk_types records which of the five risk fields apply to a run (Figure 8). Agreement is Cohen’s κ\kappa per field, between the two human ratings of a double-rated run and between a human rating and the model rating of the same run (Figure 8).

Agreement by role. For ai_misalignment, human and model ratings are identical in 99%99\% of risk runs, 96%96\% of adoption, 94%94\% of governance, 91%91\% of other roles, and 96%96\% of none. For work_roles, all values of a run agree in 76%76\% of risk runs, 62%62\% of adoption, and 48%48\% of governance.

Revision. Three parts of the taxonomy were revised on this sample after the rating: the role criteria, the examples for substantiveness, and the disclosure traits. Model–human agreement on work_roles was 0.500.50 before the revision, 0.550.55 after it, and 0.630.63 after the re-run. Two alternatives were tested and not adopted. Splitting the model rating into two calls, one for the AI-reference decision and the roles and one for the dependent fields, gave the same agreement on roles at the cost of an extra call. Replacing the substantiveness rating by a count of ten checkable particulars, mapped to three levels, reached κ=0.22\kappa{=}0.22, against 0.350.35 for the five-point rating mapped to the same three levels.
